analysis.one_liner: Requires banks to tell customers about data breaches, while overriding state breach laws.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 15, 2022, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and died there without a hearing or vote when the 117th Congress ended three weeks later.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend a 1999 banking law (the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act) to require federal financial regulators to write rules forcing banks and similar companies to tell customers when a data breach is likely to cause identity theft, fraud, or financial loss. At the same time, it would preempt—meaning wipe out—state laws on how financial companies secure personal data and notify people of breaches, replacing them with a single national standard set by federal regulators. The bill got no action beyond its referral to committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Customers of banks and other financial companies would gain a federally required notice when a breach of their data is likely to cause identity theft, fraud, or economic loss. Banks and other regulated companies would also benefit, because they would deal with one federal standard instead of fifty different state laws on data security and breach notification.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Bank customers, and the banks themselves

how_it_helps.text: Requires each federal financial regulator to ensure its rules include a breach notice whenever unauthorized access to customer data is reasonably likely to result in identity theft, fraud, or economic loss.

Adds this notification duty to Section 501 of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, the law that governs how financial companies must safeguard customer information, giving breach notice a place in the national financial-privacy framework.

Frames itself as providing 'a national standard for financial institution data security and breach notification on behalf of all consumers,' which supporters argue is simpler and more consistent than a patchwork of state rules.

analysis.who_pays: Financial institutions—banks, credit unions, and similar regulated companies—would bear the cost of monitoring for breaches and sending notifications, and of complying with new federal standards. Consumers in states with stronger data-security or breach-notification laws would give up those protections, since the bill overrides state rules for financial institutions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Financial institutions, and consumers in strict-law states

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts any state law on how financial institutions secure personal information or notify people of unauthorized access, meaning a single federal standard set by regulators would replace state rules even where state protections are tougher.
The quality of the protection would depend entirely on rules written later by federal regulators; if those rules were weak, they would be the only rules, and states could not set a higher bar.

Nearly every state already has a breach-notification law, so the bill's consumer gain over the status quo is modest, while the loss of state authority over data security for financial institutions is concrete.

A fair objection from supporters' side: fifty inconsistent state requirements can burden companies and make compliance uneven, so a uniform national rule has real appeal—though this bill settles that tradeoff in favor of the federal floor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a genuine consumer protection—a required breach notice for financially harmful breaches—with a broad preemption of state law that could leave consumers worse off in states with stronger rules than whatever federal regulators write. Because state breach-notification laws already exist nearly everywhere, the notification mandate adds little on its own, while the preemption permanently narrows state oversight of how financial companies protect personal data. As drafted, the tradeoff leans toward industry uniformity rather than maximum consumer protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the 117th Congress and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Blaine Luetkemeyer introduced the bill on December 15, 2022, with six Republican colleagues signing on as original cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, the committee with jurisdiction over banking law.
No further action was ever taken: no subcommittee or full committee markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the status quo held: consumers kept their state breach-notification protections rather than a federal standard that could be weaker, and banks avoided both the new federal compliance duty and, equally, did not get the state-law preemption they would have gained. Nobody's position changed; the main beneficiaries of the outcome are whoever preferred no change, on both sides.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo, on both sides

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors were Republicans and no Democrat cosponsored; the Democratic-chaired Financial Services Committee took no action on the bill before the Congress ended.

industries.note: The bill would hand these companies a single federal standard and wipe out state data-security and breach-notification laws for financial institutions, including stricter ones. The required customer notification roughly matches what state laws already demand, so the industry's main gain is preemption of state authority rather than a new duty.

industries.industry: State regulators and state attorneys general
industries.note: State governments would lose the power to set or enforce data-security and breach-notification standards for financial institutions, leaving enforcement to federal regulators. State authority is one of the main ways consumers currently get protection stronger than the federal floor.
